title: pip and Virtual Environments
intro:
Packages that aren't in the standard library — like `requests` or `pandas` — are installed with **pip**. A **virtual environment** (venv) is a private folder of packages for one project, so projects don't clash. In a terminal:

```
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate      # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install requests==2.32.3
pip freeze > requirements.txt
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

These commands run in a terminal, not in Python code, so the questions below practise the ideas and the files they produce.

questions.prompt: Inside an active venv, `sys.prefix` differs from `sys.base_prefix`. A **pinned** requirement like `requests==2.32.3` installs exactly that version, so everyone gets the same setup.
questions.exampleCode:
import sys
print(sys.version_info.major)
print("In a virtual environment:", sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix)
line = "requests==2.32.3"
print(line.split("=="))
questions.explanation: `requirements.txt` is just a text file with one requirement per line.

questions.prompt: `line` is a pinned requirement like `requests==2.32.3`. Split it into `name` and `version`.

tests.name: values
tests.code: assert (name, version) == tuple(line.split('==')), 'name and version should be the two parts around ==.'

questions.explanation: Requirement files are plain text, so string methods are all you need.

options.text: Creates a virtual environment in a folder called `.venv`

questions.explanation: It creates an empty, private environment; activate it before installing packages.

questions.prompt: `text` holds a requirements file. Build `packages`, a dictionary mapping each package name to its pinned version. Skip blank lines and lines starting with `#`, and ignore lines without `==`.
questions.setupCode:
text = """# web
requests==2.32.3

flask==3.0.3
pytest
# maths
numpy==1.26.4
"""

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert packages == {'requests': '2.32.3', 'flask': '3.0.3', 'numpy': '1.26.4'}, 'packages should map each pinned name to its version, skipping comments, blanks and unpinned lines.'

questions.hint: Loop over `splitlines()`, `strip()` each line, `continue` past the ones to skip.
questions.explanation: Parsing config files line by line is a very common task.

questions.prompt: Fill in the pip command that installs everything listed in a requirements file.
questions.hint: The same word you use to install one package.
questions.explanation: `-r` tells `pip install` to read names from a file.

questions.prompt: `newer` should be True because version 2.10.0 is newer than 2.9.1, but comparing the text gives False. Fix it by comparing tuples of numbers.
questions.solution:
a = "2.10.0"
b = "2.9.1"
newer = tuple(int(p) for p in a.split(".")) > tuple(int(p) for p in b.split("."))

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert newer is True, 'newer should be True: 2.10.0 is newer than 2.9.1.'

questions.hint: As text, `"1"` < `"9"`, so `"2.10"` < `"2.9"`. Compare numbers instead.
questions.explanation: Tuples compare item by item, which matches how version numbers work.
The same splitting trick works for any operator.

questions.prompt: Write `version_tuple(v)` that turns `"1.2.10"` into `(1, 2, 10)`. Then store the newest version in `versions` in `latest`.

tests.name: tuple
tests.code: assert version_tuple('1.2.10') == (1, 2, 10) and version_tuple('3') == (3,), 'version_tuple("1.2.10") should be (1, 2, 10).'
tests.message: Convert to a tuple of ints.

tests.name: latest
tests.code: assert latest == '1.10.2', 'latest should be the newest version: 1.10.2.'

questions.explanation: Passing your own function as a key is the same idea as `key=len`.

questions.prompt: Why use a separate virtual environment for each project?

options.text: So each project keeps its own package versions without clashing
It's required to run any script

questions.hint: Two projects might need different versions of the same package.
questions.explanation: A venv keeps each project's packages separate and reproducible.

questions.prompt: `installed` maps package names to versions. Build `requirements_txt`: one `name==version` line per package, sorted by name ignoring case, joined with new lines.
questions.solution:
lines = [f"{name}=={version}" for name, version in sorted(installed.items(), key=lambda item: item[0].lower())]
requirements_txt = "\n".join(lines)

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert requirements_txt == 'Flask==3.0.3\nnumpy==1.26.4\nrequests==2.32.3', 'Expected one name==version line per package, sorted by name ignoring case.'
tests.message: Check the lines and their order.

questions.hint: Sort the items by lowercase name, format each, then `"\n".join(…)`.
questions.explanation: This is what `pip freeze` produces for you.
